stories.head: Paraguay's Congress pursues Peña impeachment despite his resignation
stories.say: Paraguay's president Santiago Peña tried to resign on Thursday over the collapse of Ueno Bank, but Congress pressed ahead with impeachment and the Senate opened his trial.
stories.stand: Santiago Peña quit over the collapse of Ueno Bank, but Congress did not accept it and the Senate has opened an impeachment trial.
body: Paraguay's president, Santiago Peña, announced his resignation on Thursday after the collapse of the digital lender Ueno Bank. Congress did not accept it, and lawmakers pressed ahead with impeachment.

Al Jazeera reported that a joint session lost quorum when Colorado Party lawmakers walked out, so the resignation could not be formally accepted. El Tiempo reported that the Chamber of Deputies unanimously approved impeachment charges and the Senate began the trial on Thursday.

The central bank closed Ueno on Tuesday after its solvency ratio fell below the legal requirement. The bank had about 3 million customers and held about $850m in public funds, including pension money, Euronews and Al Jazeera reported.

The charges include poor performance of duties and conflict of interest. Peña says he sold his stake in Ueno's parent company in 2025. Al Jazeera said central bank head Carlos Carvallo has resigned, and Vice President Pedro Alliana would likely take over if Peña is removed.

stories.head: Hoax bomb threats disrupt dozens of flights across Europe
stories.say: A second wave of hoax bomb threats in a week hit flights across Europe on Thursday. Planes were diverted or escorted by fighter jets, but no explosives were found.
stories.stand: Planes were diverted, escorted or searched on Thursday in the second wave of fake threats in a week; no explosives were found.
body: Hoax bomb threats disrupted flights across Europe on Thursday, the second such wave in a week. Searches found no explosives on any aircraft, officials in several countries said.

France's prime minister's office said an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was escorted by fighter jets to the Evreux air base. All 151 passengers and six crew got off safely. Three Sofia-bound Ryanair flights made emergency landings in Bulgaria, and one from London was diverted to Plovdiv.

Czech police said a threat named four aircraft heading to Prague but rated it low. Spanish police said three emailed threats arrived within 20 minutes, affecting Air Europa and Iberia flights, Daily Maverick reported, citing Reuters.

On Tuesday, at least seven flights received similar threats, which the UK government called hoaxes. Nobody has claimed responsibility. Denmark, Poland and Romania have previously blamed Russia for hybrid attacks; Moscow denies such accusations.

stories.head: Hundreds of thousands march in France in nationwide strike
stories.say: Hundreds of thousands marched across France on Thursday in a strike over pay and living costs. Police fired tear gas in Lyon, and the prime minister meets unions on Monday.
stories.stand: Unions called the day of action over wages and living costs; police fired tear gas in Lyon, and union talks are set for Monday.
body: Workers and students marched in cities across France on Thursday in a nationwide strike called by unions including the CGT. They are demanding higher wages, a higher minimum wage and better public services.
The interior ministry put turnout at about 600,000, while the CGT said about 1.6 million took part, CBS News reported. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed.
In Lyon, police fired tear gas and reported clashes with about 500 demonstrators; six arrests were reported, Euronews said. In Paris, protesters burned objects near Place de la Nation.
The protests began in September among students angry about school conditions. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has called a meeting with unions on Monday, and another protest is planned for Saturday.

stories.head: Melania Trump hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials at White House
stories.say: Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian envoys at the White House on Thursday, urging them to build on the short Oleshky truce and seek a more enduring peace.
stories.stand: The first lady urged both sides to build on the Oleshky truce she says she brokered; new talks are expected in Abu Dhabi next week.
body: Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House on Thursday. She urged both sides to build on a recent local ceasefire in occupied Oleshky and seek a more lasting peace.

Russia was represented by Kirill Dmitriev, Vladimir Putin's special envoy. Ukraine sent David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in parliament, and human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets.

The six-day truce in the Kherson region allowed aid deliveries and the evacuation of nearly 800 people, Al Jazeera reported. It expired on Sunday without an extension. Melania Trump said both countries had accepted her as an exclusive intermediary.

Dmitriev said Putin appreciated Donald Trump's peace efforts. Arakhamia called the truce the biggest de-escalation since 2022. Al Jazeera reported that new US-brokered talks are expected in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November.

stories.head: Newsom commutes all 548 death sentences in California
stories.say: California's governor, Gavin Newsom, says he will commute the sentences of all 548 people on the state's death row to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
stories.stand: The governor says every death sentence will become life without parole; many cases still need California Supreme Court review.
body: California governor Gavin Newsom announced on Thursday that he will commute the sentences of all 548 people on the state's death row. Each will instead serve life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In an open letter, Newsom said state-sanctioned killing was incompatible with California's values. He imposed a moratorium on executions in 2019, and the state's last execution was in 2006.

The move does not repeal the death penalty, and prosecutors can still seek it. Cases involving people with more than one felony conviction need California Supreme Court review; Al Jazeera put these at about two-thirds.
Los Angeles County district attorney Nathan Hochman said only the legislature or voters could abolish the death penalty. Newsom's term ends in January 2027.

stories.head: Indiana, Florida and Alabama carry out executions on the same day
stories.say: Indiana, Florida and Alabama each executed a prisoner on Thursday, the second time this year that three US executions have taken place on the same day.
stories.stand: It was the second day this year with three US executions, and came as California announced it would empty its death row.
body: Three US states carried out executions by lethal injection on Thursday. It was the second day this year with three executions, after 13 August.

Indiana executed Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, at 12:45am at Indiana State Prison. He set a 2010 house fire that killed his girlfriend's two young children. Governor Mike Braun declined to commute his sentence.
Florida executed Jesse Guardado, 64, who pleaded guilty to stabbing a 75-year-old woman to death in 2004. Fox News said it was Florida's 19th execution this year, matching its 2025 record.

Alabama executed Michael Taylor, 54, for beating an older couple to death in a 1991 robbery when he was 19. A judge rejected his lawyers' objections to lethal injection. Fox News put the US total for 2026 at 35.

stories.head: Cuban journalist Yoani Sánchez held for hours in Havana, then freed
stories.say: Cuban journalist Yoani Sánchez was detained by state security in Havana on Thursday and released hours later. She says she is accused of attacking the constitutional order.
stories.stand: The founder of 14ymedio says she is accused of attacking the constitutional order; press freedom groups and the US condemned her detention.
body: Cuban journalist Yoani Sánchez, founder of the independent news site 14ymedio, was detained in Havana on Thursday morning and released later that day.

14ymedio said she was taken by the political police as she left her home in Nuevo Vedado to go shopping. After her release she said she had been accused of attacking the constitutional order, CiberCuba reported.

Sánchez called the detention arbitrary and thanked supporters for their solidarity. Amnesty International, Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists condemned it, as did US official Juan Pablo Segura.
Two CubaNet contributors were detained earlier in the week. Henry Constantín, who runs La Hora de Cuba, has been held since September on a disobedience charge.

stories.head: Holocaust survivor shot in Bondi attack dies, taking toll to 16
stories.say: Eva Geller, a 90-year-old Holocaust survivor shot in last December's Bondi Beach terror attack, has died in hospital in Sydney, taking the death toll to 16.
stories.stand: Eva Geller, 90, never fully recovered from wounds suffered when gunmen attacked a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi in December 2025.
body: Eva Geller, a 90-year-old Holocaust survivor wounded in the Bondi Beach terror attack, died in hospital in Sydney on Thursday night. Her death takes the toll from the attack to 16.
Two gunmen opened fire on a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi on 14 December 2025, killing 15 people. Sajid Akram was shot dead by police; his son, Naveed Akram, faces murder and terrorism charges.

Rabbi Aron Moss told ABC News she never fully recovered and was admitted to the Prince of Wales Hospital a couple of weeks ago. The Executive Council of Australian Jewry said she developed an infection from her wounds.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said her life was changed forever by terror and antisemitism. NSW Police said they were working with the coroner. A royal commission on antisemitism is due to report on 18 December.

stories.head: Pilot whales die in mass stranding on New Zealand's North Island
stories.say: Rescuers in New Zealand could not save a pod of stranded pilot whales near Cape Palliser on Thursday. The last four survivors died, including two that had been refloated.
stories.stand: Two pods came ashore near Cape Palliser on the Wairarapa coast; the last survivors died on Thursday evening despite a refloating attempt.
body: Two pods of pilot whales stranded at Ngawi, near Cape Palliser on the south-east tip of New Zealand's North Island, on Thursday.

The Department of Conservation said four whales in the first pod of about 20 were still alive and prepared a refloat at high tide. Euronews reported that two were refloated, but by the evening all four survivors had died.
Medics from the charity Project Jonah worked with conservation staff, local iwi and volunteers. Residents counted close to 50 whales, and rescuers warned some carcasses had been swept out to sea.
The conservation department said the cause had not been established. The area had not recorded a mass stranding since the 1990s, it said.

stories.head: Iran says tankers caught fire after hitting mines near Hormuz
stories.say: Iranian forces say several tankers and a tugboat caught fire near the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, most after hitting naval mines. The claims have not been independently verified.
stories.stand: Iranian forces say several tankers and a tugboat were hit in separate incidents; no ships were named and the claims are unverified.
body: Iranian forces said on Thursday that several tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents near the Strait of Hormuz.

The Revolutionary Guards said one tanker hit a mine while using what they called an illegal route south of the strait. A supertanker caught fire leaving the strait, and a tug fighting that fire also caught fire. Al Jazeera reported that Iran's army said three more tankers hit mines.
No ship names were released and the claims have not been independently verified. Separately, the UK maritime agency UKMTO said a tanker was hit by two projectiles north of Qatar late on Wednesday.
Iran has severely restricted traffic through the strait since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February, Al Jazeera reported. Qatar is mediating to resume talks.

stories.head: Somalia's top court rules president's term extension unlawful
stories.say: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's one-year term extension is unlawful, and that he should have left office in May.
stories.stand: The Supreme Court says Hassan Sheikh Mohamud should have left office in May, after he moved to dismiss the chief justice.
body: Somalia's Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's one-year term extension was unlawful. It said constitutional amendments passed in March did not apply to his term, which ended in May.
Arab News, citing AFP, reported that the court called for a new agreement among political parties within 30 days and elections within 90 days.

Before the ruling was published, Mohamud's office announced he was dismissing Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed. The court said he had no authority to do so. Former prime minister Hassan Ali Khaire said troops had been sent to the court; AFP could not verify this.
Mohamud says the extension is lawful and allows preparations for nationwide elections due in 2027. Opponents call it a power grab.

stories.head: Clashes in southern Ethiopia drive tens of thousands into Kenya
stories.say: Fighting over the Ethiopian border town of Moyale has driven about 50,000 people into Kenya, and the Kenyan Red Cross says stray bullets have killed three people in Kenya.
stories.stand: Fighting over the border town of Moyale has pushed about 50,000 people into Kenya, and stray bullets have killed three on the Kenyan side.
body: Clashes over the border town of Moyale in southern Ethiopia have driven tens of thousands of people into Kenya. Local authorities say about 50,000 have crossed, Africanews reported.

Ethiopian Somalis and Oromos have been fighting for control of the town since 18 October. Borkena reported that the fighting involves regional forces and allied militias from the Oromia and Somali regions.

The UN refugee agency says at least 11,000 displaced people, mainly women and children, are in temporary sites such as schools. The Kenyan Red Cross says stray bullets have killed three people in Kenya and wounded 20.
Separately, fighting broke out weeks earlier in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region.

stories.head: West Bank farmers harvest olives under army limits amid settler attacks
stories.say: Palestinian villagers in al-Mughayyir in the occupied West Bank say they can reach only a fraction of their olive groves, as the UN reports a record wave of settler attacks.
stories.stand: Villagers in al-Mughayyir say they can reach only a fraction of their land, as the UN records the most settler attacks since 2006.
body: Palestinian families in al-Mughayyir, north-east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, picked olives on Thursday under Israeli military restrictions. Villagers say they can reach only about 100 of their roughly 4,300 hectares.
Euronews reported that access needs prior army approval, with age limits and a ban on equipment. Footage showed troops firing tear gas near the pickers.

The UN has recorded 377 settler attacks causing casualties or damage since September, the highest since records began in 2006. Al Jazeera reported that settlers set fire to olive trees in Burqa, near Ramallah, and farmers said Israeli forces stopped them putting out the fires.

In Beit Ummar, near Hebron, Israeli security forces arrested two Israelis after settlers burned Palestinian vehicles, The Jerusalem Post reported. A day later, an Israeli vehicle was reportedly set alight in the town.

stories.head: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults
stories.say: A jury at Southwark Crown Court has convicted Russell Brand of one rape and three sexual assaults against four women. He was remanded in custody and will be sentenced on Monday.
stories.stand: The 51-year-old was cleared of two further rape counts and remanded in custody; the judge said a significant prison term was inevitable.
body: Russell Brand, 51, was found guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court in London. The jury's verdicts were unanimous, the Metropolitan Police said.
He was acquitted of two further rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. The rape he was convicted of took place at his home in 2009, Al Jazeera and CBS News reported.
Judge Joel Bennathan remanded Brand in custody and said a significant custodial term was inevitable. The Met said sentencing will take place on Monday 9 November.
Brand had denied all the charges. The Met said its investigation began after media reports of allegations in September 2023, and urged any other potential victims to come forward.

stories.head: Police car set alight as crews attacked with fireworks in Glasgow
stories.say: A police car was set alight in Glasgow on Bonfire Night after police and ambulance crews attending an injured man were targeted with fireworks. A man has been arrested.
stories.stand: Police Scotland's biggest deployment since last year's Trump visit faced disorder in Glasgow and Edinburgh on Thursday night.
body: Police and ambulance crews were attacked with fireworks on Greenside Street in Glasgow at about 7.55pm on Thursday, Police Scotland said. They had been called to a report of an injured man.
A police vehicle was set alight and badly damaged. One ambulance worker suffered a minor injury, and one man was arrested in connection with the incident.

In south Edinburgh, firefighters withdrew from bin fires because of anti-social behaviour, and fireworks were set off towards officers in Oxgangs, PA Media reported. It said seven people had been arrested in total.
Operation Amberlight was Police Scotland's largest deployment since US President Donald Trump's visit last year, with officers sent from forces in England and Wales.

stories.head: Henry Nowak's killer has minimum term raised to 25 years
stories.say: The Court of Appeal has raised the minimum term for Vickrum Digwa, who murdered student Henry Nowak in Southampton, from twenty-one to twenty-five years, ruling it unduly lenient.
stories.stand: The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient; judges rejected Digwa's own appeal that it was excessive.
body: The Court of Appeal on Thursday increased the minimum term of Vickrum Digwa's life sentence from 21 years to 25 years. He murdered 18-year-old student Henry Nowak in Southampton on 3 December 2025.
Attorney General Ellie Reeves referred the case under the Unduly Lenient Sentence Scheme. Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr, sitting with two other judges, agreed the original term was unduly lenient.
Digwa, 23, had also appealed, arguing his sentence was manifestly excessive. He watched by video link from HMP Frankland.
Digwa filmed Mr Nowak as he lay dying and falsely claimed he had been racially abused, ITV News reported. Police body-worn footage showing officers handcuffing Mr Nowak sparked protests.
Mr Nowak's family have criticised the planned early release in December of Digwa's mother, Kiran Kaur, ITV News reported. She was jailed for three years for hiding the knife.

stories.say: Councils and mayors in England could license hire e-bike schemes, with rules on parking, drunk riding and pavement riding, under plans put out for consultation on Thursday.
stories.stand: A Department for Transport consultation proposes national standards for operators such as Lime, Voi and Forest, and more control for London.
body: The Department for Transport launched a consultation on Thursday on giving councils and mayors in England powers to license shared e-bike schemes.

Operators such as Lime, Voi and Forest would have to set out parking and fleet plans, and plans to tackle drunk riding, underage riding and riding on pavements. They may also face insurance requirements.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the government could not legislate for every rider but could give local leaders more control. She is working with London mayor Sadiq Khan on giving Transport for London similar powers.
Mr Khan welcomed the plans, saying he had sought powers since the first dockless schemes arrived in London in 2017. Lime's chief executive called the consultation an important step.

stories.head: Met chief calls for 43 police forces to merge into eight to 10
stories.say: Sir Mark Rowley is calling for England and Wales's 43 police forces to be replaced by eight to ten regional forces, warning that policing is heading for failure without reform.
stories.stand: In a speech in Manchester on Friday, the Metropolitan Police Commissioner backs regional forces and a new National Police Service.
body: Sir Mark Rowley, Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, is to call for the 43 police forces in England and Wales to be replaced by eight to 10 regional forces, the Met said.
In a speech in Manchester on Friday alongside four other police chiefs, he proposes three tiers: local policing teams, regional forces and a new National Police Service for the most serious crimes.
The Met says Sir Mark will argue that removing duplication would free thousands of roles for frontline work. He says crime networks work across borders while policing is organised locally.
He cites policing spending falling from about 0.9% of GDP to about 0.7% since 2010, and public confidence falling by nine percent.

stories.say: Councils in England can now apply to take over the management of homes left empty for six months, down from two years, under rules that took effect on Thursday.
stories.stand: Changes to Empty Dwelling Management Orders apply to applications made from 5 November; a tribunal must still approve each order.
body: Councils in England can now seek Empty Dwelling Management Orders for homes left empty for six months, down from two years. The change applies to applications made on or after 5 November.
Councils no longer have to show that an empty property is causing a nuisance or that the local community supports an order, Propertymark said.
Under an order, the council manages and can let the property without taking ownership. An interim order must be authorised by the First-tier Tribunal, and owners must be notified in advance.
Existing exemptions remain, including homes being marketed for sale or let and some second homes. Propertymark says more than 359,000 UK homes have been empty for over six months.

stories.say: Cyclists are breaking the new traffic ban on London's Oxford Street on average every five minutes, according to ITV News filming, but no one has yet been fined.
stories.stand: All traffic was banned from the street about ten days earlier; cyclists face a possible £160 penalty but none have been issued.
body: ITV News filmed Oxford Street for an hour in both the morning and evening rush hours and recorded a cyclist breaking the new rules on average every five minutes.
All traffic was banned from the London shopping street about ten days earlier. Cycling there carries a possible £160 penalty, but ITV News said no one had been fined so far.
Transport for London said 400 to 500 cyclists an hour used the street at peak times before pedestrianisation, and that numbers had fallen significantly.
Lime said its hire bikes were barred from riding and parking in the zone, though some were still getting through. The London Cycling Campaign said alternative routes were poorly designed for bikes.

body: Syed Ahmed, 38, a maths teacher in Essex, was jailed for 10 years on Thursday for grooming and sexually abusing teenage girls, LBC reported.
He used a false name, false age and heavily filtered photos on apps including Snapchat, Wizz and Yubo to pose as a teenage boy. The girls were aged 13 to 16 and none attended his school.
Five of the girls were persuaded to meet him in person. He was convicted after a trial in June and July, and had admitted further offences including sexual communication with a child.
In September 2025 he received an extended sentence over separate offences at Southwark Crown Court, the Crown Prosecution Service said. He resigned from teaching after his arrest in May 2023.

stories.stand: The gang broke into a lorry at a Northampton layby to grab holdalls of cocaine shipped from Mexico through Felixstowe, the Met said.
body: Three people have been jailed for a total of more than 47 years for trying to smuggle 780kg of cocaine into the UK, the Metropolitan Police said. Its street value was over £80 million.
Craig Le-Mare, 36, was sentenced to 20 years on Wednesday after being convicted at the Old Bailey. Michael Weston, 57, and Kelly Robertson, 46, had earlier pleaded guilty and were jailed.
The drugs were hidden in a container of steel furniture parts that left Mexico and arrived at Felixstowe port. The gang followed the lorry to a layby in Northampton and broke into the container.
Bystanders saw them and they fled. Northamptonshire Police recovered 18 holdalls in total from the lorry and a van.

body: Democrats flipped five Republican-held US House seats in North Carolina in Tuesday's midterm elections, WRAL and WUNC reported.

Richard Ojeda, an Army veteran, defeated Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee. Cyril Jefferson, Paul Barringer and Lakesha Womack beat Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, and Jamie Ager won an open seat.
Ojeda, who opposed the Iran war, won a district Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, WRAL reported. Republican Virginia Foxx trailed by about 100 votes in a race heading for a possible recount.
Across the country, CBS News counted 43 House districts that had moved to Democrats and two to Republicans, with dozens of races still to be projected.

stories.head: ANC heads for new low as DA claims outright win in Cape Town
stories.say: Partial results in South Africa's local elections put the ANC on about 32 percent and the DA on 25. DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis has declared an outright win in Cape Town.
stories.stand: Partial results in South Africa's local elections put the ANC on about 32% and the DA second; final results are expected on Sunday.
body: Partial results from South Africa's local elections put the African National Congress on about 32%, with the Democratic Alliance on 25% and MK on 8.5%, Al Jazeera reported. The ANC won just over 40% in the 2024 national election.

DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis declared an outright win in Cape Town on Thursday, Daily Maverick reported. Projections showed the DA well short of a majority in Johannesburg, where coalitions look likely.
The ANC lost control of Makana municipality in the Eastern Cape for the first time in its history, Daily Maverick reported. The party is disputing how seats there were allocated.
Turnout was about 54.5%, up from 46% in 2021. Final results are expected on Sunday.

stories.head: Milei and Sánchez exchange cold greeting at Madrid summit
stories.say: Javier Milei and Pedro Sánchez exchanged a brief, distant greeting at the Ibero-American summit in Madrid, two weeks after Argentina's president called Spain's prime minister a dictator.
stories.stand: Argentina's president skipped the summit opening and the royal gala, and did not meet King Felipe VI, amid a long-running row with Spain's prime minister.
body: Argentina's president, Javier Milei, and Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, exchanged a brief and distant greeting at the 30th Ibero-American Summit in Madrid on Thursday, Euronews reported.
It came two weeks after Milei called Sánchez a dictator. Spain withdrew its ambassador from Buenos Aires in May 2024 after Milei criticised Sánchez and his wife at an event run by the Vox party.
Milei skipped the summit's opening and the gala dinner hosted by the king and queen, La Nación reported. Shortly after arriving he met Vox leader Santiago Abascal.
El Mundo reported that Argentina had asked, through Sánchez's office, for an audience with King Felipe VI. Argentine presidency sources denied a formal request was made, and no meeting took place.

stories.say: More government files on Peter Mandelson's appointment as ambassador to Washington are due out by Christmas, after the Metropolitan Police agreed they could be released.
stories.stand: The Metropolitan Police has let the government release files it had held back during its investigation into Lord Mandelson.
body: More government files on Lord Peter Mandelson's appointment as US ambassador are expected to be published by Christmas, City AM reported.

Senior civil servant Cat Little told MPs in a letter that the Metropolitan Police had allowed the release of files previously held back. The Met had asked for them to be withheld during its investigation into allegations that Mandelson leaked sensitive information to Jeffrey Epstein.
MPs on a security committee will redact anything that could harm national security or international relations. Earlier batches were published in March and June.
Mandelson was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office and released on bail. The releases follow a Commons motion brought by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch.

stories.head: Farage blames Iran war for Republicans' midterm defeat
stories.say: Nigel Farage has called the Republicans' midterm results a disaster, blaming Donald Trump for breaking his promise of no more foreign wars. He fears Trump will keep attacking Iran.
stories.stand: The Reform UK leader called the results a disaster and said he feared Trump would keep attacking Iran, pushing up oil prices and inflation.
body: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told reporters on Thursday that the Republicans' midterm results were a disaster, PoliticsHome reported.
He blamed Donald Trump for breaking his promise of no more foreign wars, pointing to the war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and higher fuel prices.
Farage said he had backed the initial US decision to attack Iran but never supported endless war. He said he feared Trump would keep attacking Iran, which could push up oil prices and inflation.

Farage, who calls himself a friend and ally of Trump, said he had wrongly predicted smaller losses. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the results offered a chance to end the war and tackle the cost of living.

stories.head: Nigerian court voids Atiku Abubakar's opposition presidential candidacy
stories.say: A Nigerian court has cancelled Atiku Abubakar's nomination as the opposition ADC's presidential candidate, two months before the election. The party says it will appeal.
stories.stand: A Federal High Court ruling sacked the ADC's leadership and cancelled its nominations two months before the presidential election; the party will appeal.
body: Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court in Abuja on Thursday nullified Atiku Abubakar's nomination as presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, Pulse Nigeria and Tribune reported.

The court upheld a case by Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former deputy national chairman, who disputed the party leadership of David Mark. It ruled the Mark-led leadership unlawful and voided its actions, including nominations for the 2027 elections.

The ADC said it would appeal. Its spokesman described the ruling as an attempt to weaken the opposition and accused the governing APC of involvement, which a spokesman for President Tinubu denied, Africanews reported.
The presidential election is due on 16 January 2027. Abubakar came second in 2023 with 29% of the vote.

stories.head: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% as energy costs push up inflation
stories.say: The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4%, its first rise since 2023. It expects inflation to climb to about 5% by the middle of next year as energy costs surge.
stories.stand: The first rise since 2023 follows a jump in energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict; the Bank expects inflation to peak around 5%.
body: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% on Thursday. It is the first increase since August 2023.
Eight of the nine Monetary Policy Committee members voted for the rise. Catherine Mann voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%.
The Bank said energy prices had risen sharply because of the Middle East conflict. Inflation was 3.5% in September, and the Bank's staff expect it to reach about 5% in the second quarter of 2027.

Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise should not be seen as the first in a long, inevitable series, MoneyWeek reported. But he said another rise looked likely unless the conflict is resolved. The next decision is due on 17 December.

stories.say: Borrowers on tracker mortgages face higher monthly bills after Thursday's rate rise, and about 2.3 million households come off fixed-rate deals by the end of 2027.
stories.stand: Tracker repayments rise almost at once, while about 2.3 million households come off fixed-rate deals by the end of 2027.
body: Homeowners on tracker mortgages will see repayments rise almost immediately after the Bank of England raised rates to 4% on Thursday. UK Finance puts the average increase at £30.72 a month, City AM reported.
Moneyfacts estimates the quarter-point rise adds about £37 a month to a £250,000 tracker mortgage over 25 years, according to MoneyWeek.
About 2.3 million households come off fixed-rate deals by the end of 2027, City AM said. Fixed-rate borrowers are unaffected until their deal ends, and many lenders had already priced in the rise.
Moneyfacts puts the average five-year fixed rate at 6%. A City AM/Freshwater Strategy poll found 29% of people believe they could not afford the increase.

stories.stand: The German defence company now expects 2026 sales of about €13.2 billion, blaming a delayed army vehicle order and slower ammunition acceptance.
body: Rheinmetall shares fell more than 15% on Thursday after the German defence company cut its 2026 targets for the second time this year.
It now expects sales of about €13.2 billion, down from €13.7 billion to €14.2 billion. Its operating margin target was cut to about 18.5% from about 19%, and it dropped a cash-generation goal.

The company said a large German armoured vehicle order, known as Arminius, was no longer expected this year, pushing sales into 2027. Slower acceptance of artillery ammunition batches also delayed revenue.
Third-quarter operating profit rose 62% to €553 million, beating forecasts, but sales of €3.15 billion missed expectations, Investing.com reported.

Its net profit forecast rose to 3.57 trillion yen from 3.25 trillion yen, according to Jiji Press via Nippon.com. The company lowered its sales projection to 53.5 trillion yen.

body: Wendy's rejected a $1.4 billion takeover proposal on Thursday from an investor group led by Trian Partners, the firm founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz.

stories.stand: The Treasury says an India-based network gave false flags to ships carrying Iranian oil, and a Turkish firm served sanctioned Iranian airlines.
body: The US Treasury announced sanctions on Wednesday against people and companies in India and Turkey that it accuses of helping Iran evade restrictions.

It said a network run by India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and Jaspreet Preeti Shahid provided false flags and fake certifications to sanctioned vessels carrying Iranian petroleum. The Treasury says the couple falsely claimed to represent Guyana, Eswatini and Laos.
Turkey-based Fugo Ground Services was sanctioned for providing ground handling to sanctioned Iranian airlines, including Iran Air Tour and Saha Airlines.
The measures are part of a US campaign called Operation Economic Outcast, aimed at cutting off Iran's oil revenue. India had not commented, Daily Maverick reported.

stories.say: Thailand's prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, says the US midterms will not affect a trade deal with Washington, with the US tariff on Thai goods at 19%.
stories.stand: Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul says core terms of a reciprocal trade agreement with the US are settled, and legal teams are reviewing the draft.
body: Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Thursday that the US midterm elections would not affect Thailand's planned trade agreement with the United States.

He said both sides had settled the main terms, and legal teams are checking the draft, The Nation reported. According to Thai PBS World, Anutin said the US tariff rate on Thai goods had returned to 19%.

Anutin plans to raise Thailand's request for special tariff treatment with President Donald Trump at the ASEAN and APEC summits. He said Thailand had met its commitments on peace efforts with Cambodia.
Existing tariff arrangements stay in place until the main agreement is formally signed, The Nation said.

stories.head: Blue Origin delays New Glenn's return to flight until January 2027
stories.say: Blue Origin has pushed New Glenn's return to flight back to January 2027, missing its goal of flying again this year while it rebuilds a launch pad wrecked in a May explosion.
stories.stand: The rocket has been grounded since an explosion during a test in May badly damaged its only launch pad, in Florida.
body: Blue Origin has moved the next launch of its New Glenn rocket to January 2027, missing its earlier pledge to fly again before the end of 2026.

The rocket exploded during an engine test on 28 May, destroying the vehicle and badly damaging the company's only New Glenn launch pad at Cape Canaveral, Florida. It has been grounded since. The Next Web reported that bad summer weather slowed the rebuilding work, according to chief executive Dave Limp.
In a memo to staff reported by Bloomberg, Limp said returning New Glenn to flight remained the company's top priority. The Financial Times first reported the delay.
The next flight was due to carry 48 Amazon Leo internet satellites, The Next Web reported. New Glenn has flown three times since its debut in January 2025.

stories.head: Spacewalkers fit final new solar array, completing station power upgrade
stories.say: Astronauts Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk spent nearly seven hours outside the International Space Station on Thursday, installing the last of eight new solar arrays.
stories.stand: Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk installed the eighth roll-out array on the International Space Station, finishing work that began in 2021.
body: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed and unfolded the eighth and final roll-out solar array on the International Space Station on Thursday.
The spacewalk lasted 6 hours and 59 minutes, NASA said. It was Menon's fifth spacewalk and Kutryk's second; the pair fitted the seventh array the week before.

NASA says the upgrade, begun in 2021, raises the station's power capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts. The new panels offset the decline of the original arrays after more than 20 years in space, CBS News reported.
Controllers saw less power than expected after the cables were connected. The crew rechecked the connections and the problem was resolved. The station is due to be retired in 2030.

stories.head: New software helps Webb telescope reveal a planet hidden in its data
stories.say: Astronomers say a new software model of the James Webb Space Telescope makes faint planets two to fifteen times easier to spot, and it found one that earlier processing had missed.
stories.stand: A physics-based model of the telescope, called FLIP, picked out a known giant planet that standard methods had missed in earlier Webb observations.
body: Astronomers led by Northwestern University have developed software that makes the James Webb Space Telescope up to 15 times more sensitive to planets near bright stars, according to a study in Nature.

The method, called FLIP, builds a physics-based model of Webb's camera to subtract starlight, instead of relying on images of reference stars. Universe Today and Tech Times report a sensitivity gain of 2 to 15 times over standard techniques.

Applied to existing Webb data, it revealed 51 Eridani b, a planet about three times the mass of Jupiter, which standard processing had not shown, Tech Times reported. The planet was first found with ground-based telescopes.
The lead author is Northwestern graduate student Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez. Co-authors include Jason Wang of Northwestern and Katherine Bouman of Caltech.

stories.head: Gas seeping from Martian fissures hints at dormant volcanism
stories.say: A European orbiter has detected hydrogen chloride gas above narrow fissures on the Martian volcano Alba Mons, which scientists say suggests Mars may still be volcanically active.
stories.stand: Europe's Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrogen chloride above narrow fissures on Alba Mons, which researchers link to magma beneath the surface.
body: Scientists say gas detected above cracks on the Martian volcano Alba Mons suggests Mars is volcanically dormant rather than dead. The study was published in Science Advances on Wednesday.

Instruments on the European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrogen chloride, a gas commonly released from magmatic vents on Earth. It appeared in early northern summer in the same place, above narrow fissures on the volcano's flanks.
The team proposes that the gas rises from a dormant magma chamber, is trapped under ice in winter and escapes as the ice turns to vapour. No new lava flows or eruptions have been observed on Mars.
Alexander Trokhimovskiy is lead author, and Daniel Mège of the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences co-led the work. Sci.News reported an estimated seepage rate below 3kg a second.

stories.say: India is aiming for debris-free space by 2030, minister Jitendra Singh said on Thursday, as he opened a Hyderabad facility where a start-up will build debris-clearing robots.
stories.stand: Minister Jitendra Singh opened a Hyderabad facility where start-up Cosmoserve Space will design and test robots for clearing orbital debris.
body: India is targeting a debris-free space environment by 2030, Union Minister Jitendra Singh said on Thursday.

Speaking virtually from New Delhi, Singh inaugurated Base 1, a facility of Hyderabad start-up Cosmoserve Space. It covers about 14,800 square feet and will be used to design, build, test and operate space robots for debris removal and in-orbit servicing.
Singh said India was emerging among the early pioneers in space debris removal. He put India's space economy at nearly 9 billion US dollars, with about 450 space start-ups.
Cosmoserve, led by founder Chiranjeevi Phanindra, tested soft robotic petals in space in July, News Age reported. Daily Excelsior reported total funding of over 9 million US dollars.

stories.say: Three NASA astronauts on the International Space Station, Anil Menon, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, voted in the US elections from orbit, with ballots sent down by satellite.
stories.stand: Anil Menon, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins voted from orbit, with ballots relayed by satellite to Harris County, Texas.
body: NASA astronauts Anil Menon, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins cast their votes in the US elections from the International Space Station, Euronews reported.
Menon posted a video on X showing a voting sticker and his private cabin. He filled in his ballot on a computer and sent it to Harris County, Texas, home of the Johnson Space Center.

Ballots are relayed through NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System to a ground station in New Mexico, then to Mission Control in Houston and the county election official. NASA says they are encrypted.
Astronauts have been able to vote from space since a 1997 Texas law. David Wolf was the first, from the Russian space station Mir.

stories.head: Fossil teeth reveal giant rodent that roamed Thailand 35 million years ago
stories.say: Scientists have named a new giant rodent from two fossil teeth found in a Thai coal mine. Yakamys sirindhornae weighed about thirty kilos and lived 33 to 35 million years ago.
stories.stand: Yakamys sirindhornae, named after Princess Sirindhorn, weighed about 30kg and is among the largest known rodents of its era, researchers say.
body: Researchers from Thailand, France and Canada have identified a new genus and species of giant rodent from two fossil teeth found in Krabi province, southern Thailand. The study was published in Scientific Reports.

Named Yakamys sirindhornae after Princess Sirindhorn, the animal lived 33 to 35 million years ago and weighed about 30kg, about half the weight of a large capybara. It belonged to an extinct early rodent family, the Ischyromyidae.
A molar and an incisor were found in a coal mine in 2004. Geologist Pannipa Tian of Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources found the incisor and at first took it for bone, she told AFP.
Thai PBS World reported that the team was led by Yaowalak Chaimanee of France's CNRS. With only teeth, the animal's diet and appearance remain unknown.

stories.head: CT scans crack the code of a 400-year-old lock from a Welsh shipwreck
stories.say: Researchers in Cardiff have used CT scans to crack the four-letter code of a brass combination lock from a ship wrecked off south Wales in 1583. The code spells ANCE.
stories.stand: Micro-CT imaging revealed the four-letter combination ANCE on a brass lock from a merchant ship wrecked near Port Talbot in 1583.
body: Researchers at Cardiff University and Amgueddfa Cymru, Museum Wales, have found the code of a brass combination lock recovered from a 16th-century shipwreck.

David Williams, a research associate at Cardiff University's School of Engineering, used micro-CT scanning to make a 3D image of the mechanism without damaging it. The notches showed the four-letter code ANCE, which the museum team then tested. Its meaning is unknown.

The lock came from an English merchant ship returning from Spain that was wrecked on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot, in a storm in December 1583. It was found near Spanish silver coins and probably secured a small chest.
Nation.Cymru reported that the lock is on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea until June 2027.

stories.head: Neolithic cemetery with human-shaped standing stone excavated near Paris
stories.say: French archaeologists have excavated a 6,500-year-old cemetery on the edge of Paris, with eleven graves and a carved human-shaped stone weighing nearly ten tonnes.
stories.stand: French archaeologists found 11 graves and a 9.7-tonne statue-menhir at Champigny-sur-Marne, dating to about 6,500 years ago.
body: Archaeologists from France's national preventive archaeology institute, Inrap, have excavated a Neolithic cemetery at Champigny-sur-Marne, on the south-eastern edge of Paris. It dates to about 4750 to 4300 BC.

The site holds 11 graves and 30 large stone blocks. Its centrepiece is a human-shaped statue-menhir, 3.04 metres long and weighing an estimated 9.7 tonnes, with an engraved belt and possible traces of paint.
The statue was found lying in the pit where it once stood; why it fell is unknown. One adult had been buried seated in a narrow circular pit.
Inrap says builders used a primitive cement of local sediment, gravel and water. Ancient DNA and isotope tests are planned. The site was dug ahead of property development.

stories.head: Slow gut-to-brain dopamine signal teaches mice to like nutritious foods
stories.say: Scientists in San Francisco have found a slow dopamine signal, set off by nutrients reaching the gut, that mice need in order to learn which flavours bring calories.
stories.stand: A UCSF study in Nature finds nutrients in the gut trigger lasting dopamine release in the amygdala, which mice need to learn flavour preferences.
body: Researchers at the University of California, San Francisco have identified a slow dopamine signal that helps animals learn to like foods that provide nutrients. The study was published in Nature on 4 November.

In mice, sugar or fat delivered straight into the stomach caused sustained dopamine release in the basolateral amygdala, a brain region. The signal built up after food reached the gut and could last many minutes.
Blocking the signal did not stop mice eating, but they failed to learn that a new flavour meant calories. Stimulating the same dopamine fibres made them prefer a calorie-free flavour.
Brain scans of people showed nutrient-linked activity in the same region, Sci.News reported. The senior author is Zachary Knight of UCSF.

stories.head: Cologne experiment finds signs of long-predicted protected quantum states
stories.say: Physicists in Cologne say an experiment on a topological insulator shows signs of states first predicted in 2008, which could help build more error-resistant quantum computers.
stories.stand: Physicists saw an energy gap close and reopen in a topological insulator junction, as theory predicts for states that could aid quantum computing.
body: Physicists at the University of Cologne, with theorists at RWTH Aachen University, report signs of long-predicted protected quantum states in a study in Science Advances.

The team placed aluminium strips on thin flakes of a topological insulator, a material that conducts only along its surface, and cooled them to 50 millikelvin. As a magnetic field tuned the junction, an energy gap closed and then reopened in a repeating pattern.
This matches a 2008 prediction by Liang Fu and Charles Kane, linked to Majorana states that could support topological quantum computing.
The researchers say the results are consistent with topological protection but do not prove it. Confirming the phase transition would need further measurements, Earth.com reported.

stories.say: NASA is asking companies for ideas to push the Hubble Space Telescope into a higher orbit, saying any boost mission would need to launch by 2032 to prevent re-entry.
stories.stand: With Hubble's orbit slowly decaying, NASA is seeking commercial ideas to boost or service it; a boost would need to launch by 2032.
body: NASA has asked industry for ideas on commercial missions that could boost or service the Hubble Space Telescope, which has no propulsion of its own.
Atmospheric drag is slowly lowering Hubble's orbit. NASA's current analysis puts its likely re-entry in 2033 or 2034, and a boost mission would need to launch by 2032, ScienceDaily reported.

Options include pushing the telescope higher, upgrading it, or retiring it safely. Responses to NASA's request for information, issued on 29 October, are due by 30 November. NASA has not committed to buying a mission.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said Hubble still had important science ahead of it. Tech Insider reported a target altitude of at least 600 km.

body: A UK doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working on the epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has been flown back to Britain, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday.

The doctor, who has not been named, is being cared for in a high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free Hospital in London. The government said it worked with the Congolese government and international partners on the medical evacuation flight.

ITV News reported that the outbreak, caused by Bundibugyo virus, has killed more than 5,000 people. Only four Ebola cases had previously been confirmed in the UK.

stories.head: Cancer diagnoses in England pass 1,000 a day for the first time
stories.say: For the first time, more than a thousand people a day were diagnosed with cancer in England in 2024. Prostate cancer was the most common, NHS figures show.
stories.stand: NHS England figures show 373,574 new cancer diagnoses in 2024, a record, with prostate cancer the most commonly diagnosed.
body: The NHS in England diagnosed an average of 1,021 cancers a day in 2024, up from 972 in 2023, NHS England said on Thursday. It is the first time the daily figure has passed 1,000.
There were 373,574 new diagnoses, excluding the most common skin cancers, which is 11,833 more than the year before. Prostate cancer was the most diagnosed, with 61,115 cases.

Prostate, breast, lung and bowel cancers made up about half of diagnoses. Separate monthly data show 78.6% of urgent referrals were diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days in August, below the 80% target.
Professor Peter Johnson, the NHS national clinical director for cancer, said the service was moving in the right direction and urged people to attend screening when invited.

stories.say: A baby has died of measles in Wisconsin, the state's first measles death since 1990. Officials say almost all of this year's cases there were in unvaccinated people.
stories.stand: The death is linked to an outbreak in south-west Wisconsin, where nearly all of the state's 431 cases this year were in unvaccinated people.
body: An infant has died of measles in Wisconsin, the state's Department of Health Services announced on Thursday. It is the first measles death in the state since 1990.
The department linked the death to an outbreak in south-west Wisconsin. It did not give the child's age or location, citing the family's privacy.
Wisconsin has recorded 431 measles cases this year, and all but three were in unvaccinated people, STAT and WISN reported. Nine people have been treated in hospital.
Health secretary Kirsten Johnson called any child's death from a vaccine-preventable disease a tragedy. The department says two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97% effective.

stories.say: More than twenty thousand patients in England will be offered blood tests for abdominal cancers at their GP, in a trial to see whether they help doctors spot cancer earlier.
stories.stand: The STRIDE-RCT trial will test blood tests on more than 20,000 patients aged 45 and over who see their GP with abdominal symptoms.
body: A trial of blood tests designed to detect several abdominal cancers is starting in at least 200 GP practices in England, the government and the NIHR announced this week.
The STRIDE-RCT trial, led by the University of Birmingham, will involve more than 20,000 patients aged 45 and over who see their GP with symptoms such as persistent bloating or discomfort.
The tests, which use artificial intelligence and measure blood proteins, need one or two extra tubes of blood. A positive result is not a diagnosis but could help GPs decide on urgent referrals.
The trial has £8.49 million of funding from the Office for Life Sciences. About 71,000 people in England are diagnosed with pancreatic, stomach, liver, ovarian or bowel cancer each year.

stories.head: Novartis confirms nine tumour reports in Zolgensma gene therapy patients
stories.say: Novartis has confirmed nine reports of tumours in patients given its gene therapy Zolgensma. In two, the therapy's vector had entered the patients' DNA.
stories.stand: Two of the cases in children treated for spinal muscular atrophy showed the therapy's vector had integrated into their DNA, the company says.
body: Novartis has confirmed nine reports of tumours in patients treated with Zolgensma, its gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy, BioSpace and Tech Times reported on Thursday.
Two of the cases showed evidence that the therapy's viral vector had integrated into the patients' DNA. The other seven have not been causally linked to the treatment.

The company said both patients were treated for their tumours and are being monitored, and that it notified health authorities. More than 6,000 patients have received Zolgensma since its 2019 approval.
Novartis said the potential risk of tumours from vector integration is already in the prescribing information. Patient group SMA Europe said regulators are assessing the reports.

stories.head: Cholesterol drug Repatha linked to 20% fewer heart attacks than ezetimibe
stories.say: A large study by drugmaker Amgen found patients given its cholesterol drug Repatha had a twenty per cent lower rate of heart attacks than those on the older drug ezetimibe.
stories.stand: A study of more than 544,000 US patients compared two drugs given on top of statins; it is observational and was run by Repatha's maker, Amgen.
body: Patients who started the cholesterol drug Repatha had a 20% lower rate of heart attacks than those who started ezetimibe, according to a study announced by its maker Amgen on Thursday.
The study used US health records for 544,103 adults with heart and artery disease who had already taken statins. It followed them for up to four years.

Among patients with a baseline cholesterol reading, four-year heart attack risk was 5.88% on Repatha and 7.76% on ezetimibe. The results were published in the American Journal of Preventive Cardiology.
The study was observational rather than a randomised trial, and was carried out by Amgen, which sells Repatha.

stories.head: A third of babies diagnosed with peanut allergy can eat peanuts, study finds
stories.say: Australian researchers say more than one in three babies diagnosed with peanut allergy had no reaction when given peanut in hospital. They warn parents not to try it at home.
stories.stand: Australian researchers found nearly 35% of infants with a suspected peanut allergy had no reaction in a supervised hospital food challenge.
body: Nearly 35% of infants diagnosed with peanut allergy did not react when given peanut in a supervised hospital test, a study by Australia's Murdoch Children's Research Institute has found.
The records of 1,275 babies referred to public hospitals were reviewed. The infants had reacted to peanut and tested positive on skin-prick or blood tests, LiveScience reported.
Of those who reacted during the challenge, about 12% had anaphylaxis, a severe reaction, so experts say challenges must be supervised and never tried at home.
Kirsten Perrett, director of the National Allergy Centre of Excellence, said history and allergy tests alone were not enough to diagnose many babies accurately.

stories.head: Flu and RSV edge up in England as Covid-19 falls, UKHSA says
stories.say: Flu and RSV are both rising in England, and the UK Health Security Agency expects further increases now schools are back. Covid-19, meanwhile, is falling.
stories.stand: Weekly surveillance shows flu positivity rising to 7.6% and RSV to 2.9%, while Covid-19 admissions fell; officials expect flu and RSV to rise further.
body: Flu positivity in England rose to 7.6% from 6.8% in the latest week, with hospital admissions up to 2.83 per 100,000 people, the UK Health Security Agency said on Thursday.
RSV positivity rose to 2.9% from 1.6%. Covid-19 positivity fell to 7.6%, and hospital admissions fell to 2.23 per 100,000. Norovirus remained within expected levels.
Dr Jamie Lopez Bernal, a UKHSA consultant epidemiologist, said flu cases remained low with a small rise in hospital admissions, and that flu and RSV were expected to increase now schools are back.
The agency urged eligible people to book their flu, Covid-19 and RSV vaccines.

stories.head: Medicare cuts US doctors' pay rate by 2.31% for 2027
stories.say: Medicare will cut the main payment rate for US doctors by two point three one per cent next year, a deeper cut than first proposed. Doctors' groups are urging Congress to step in.
stories.stand: The final 2027 fee schedule cuts deeper than proposed and delays a ban on outsourced remote patient monitoring until 2029.
body: The US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services finalised its 2027 physician fee schedule on Wednesday, cutting the main conversion factor by 2.31% to $32.63.
In July the agency had proposed a 1.68% cut. A one-year 2.5% increase approved by Congress for 2026 expires at the end of the year.
A proposed 50% pay cut for office visits billed on the same day as minor procedures was reduced to 20%. A ban on paying for remote monitoring done by outside vendors was delayed to 2029.
The Medical Group Management Association said the cuts weaken an already fragile payment system and called on Congress to intervene.

stories.head: Catholic takeover to end IVF and abortion at two Newcastle hospitals
stories.say: IVF, elective abortion and voluntary assisted dying will end at two private hospitals in Newcastle, Australia, once Catholic provider Calvary takes them over.
stories.stand: Calvary Health Care, buying two private hospitals in New South Wales after Healthscope's collapse, confirmed services barred by its Catholic code will stop.
body: Calvary Health Care has confirmed that IVF, elective abortions, voluntary assisted dying and gender reassignment procedures will stop at Newcastle Private Hospital and Hunter Valley Private Hospital, ABC News reported on Thursday.

Calvary, a Catholic provider, is buying the hospitals as part of a plan to take over 14 hospitals after Healthscope collapsed. It hopes to take control by the end of November, subject to regulatory approval.

Calvary says the deal will bring greater stability and most services will be kept. New South Wales Health Minister Ryan Park said the government cannot dictate private hospital services, and would look at filling gaps.
Local doctors said the public system would struggle to absorb the extra demand. Hunter IVF said its laboratory and stored eggs were not affected.

stories.head: Northern Territory health staff banned from wearing smart glasses
stories.say: Health workers in Australia's Northern Territory have been banned from wearing smart glasses at clinical sites, after a review found recording devices put patient privacy at risk.
stories.stand: NT Health says recording-capable wearables pose an elevated risk to patient privacy, after a breach at Royal Darwin Hospital in October.
body: NT Health has banned all staff from using smart glasses and other recording-capable wearables at its clinical sites, ABC News reported on Thursday.
Devices are allowed only if NT Health approves them for a legitimate purpose. An internal review found they pose an elevated risk to patient privacy and confidentiality.

The review followed a breach at Royal Darwin Hospital in October, when a medical observer posted images and videos containing confidential details of pregnant patients online. It is not suggested smart glasses were used.
Chief executive Susan Bowden told staff patient consent comes first. The Australian Medical Association in the territory supported the ban.

body: Guatemala's vice-minister for hospitals, María del Rosario Orozco, has resigned after allegations of nepotism at Hospital Roosevelt, the health ministry confirmed on Thursday.
The allegations concern the hiring of her son at the hospital. Congresswoman Evelyn Morataya raised the case at a hearing in October and called it influence peddling.
The ministry said she left for personal reasons. Health Minister Joaquín Barnoya has requested a detailed report, and the ministry said the review would continue regardless of the resignation.
Infobae reported that acting President Karin Herrera signed the decree accepting the resignation. No replacement has yet been named.

stories.head: Nearly 90 million displaced people face severe climate risks, UN says
stories.say: The UN refugee agency says nearly 90 million displaced people live in countries highly exposed to droughts, floods and extreme heat, and wants more climate finance to reach them.
stories.stand: The UN refugee agency says three-quarters of the world's forcibly displaced people live in countries highly exposed to climate hazards.
body: The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says nearly 90 million refugees and other forcibly displaced people live in countries with severe exposure to climate hazards. That is about three-quarters of the world's displaced people.

The report says more than two-thirds of refugees who returned home in the first half of 2026 went to countries highly exposed to climate hazards. In Syria, nearly 4 million displaced people have recently returned.

By 2050, one in three refugee settlements in sub-Saharan Africa could face at least 100 days of dangerous heat a year. Flooding linked to El Niño could displace up to 3 million people in Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan and Uganda by the end of 2026.

Only about 10% of climate finance reaches fragile and conflict-affected countries, the agency says. Anton Leis Garcia, a UNHCR assistant high commissioner, urged that funding go where needs are greatest. The report comes ahead of COP31 in Antalya, Turkey.

stories.head: COP31 climate talks open in Antalya on Monday as some leaders stay away
stories.say: The UN climate summit opens in Antalya, Turkey, on Monday. Japan's prime minister will skip it, while 19 US lawmakers plan to attend though Washington is not negotiating.
stories.stand: The UN summit runs from 9 to 20 November; Japan's prime minister will skip it, while 19 US lawmakers plan to attend despite Washington's absence.
body: COP31, the UN climate conference, runs from 9 to 20 November at Antalya in Turkey. Turkish environment minister Murat Kurum is COP president, while Australia manages the formal negotiations. The leaders' segment is on 11 and 12 November.

Japan's chief cabinet secretary, Minoru Kihara, said on Thursday that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi would not attend, citing scheduling reasons. Environment minister Hiroyoshi Sasagawa will represent Japan. Climate Home News reports that China and India are also not sending their top leaders.

Climate Home News says Brazil's Lula, the UK's Andy Burnham and Spain's Pedro Sánchez are on the early speakers' list. A provisional UN list cited by Climate & Capital Media shows 77 heads of state or government due to speak, against 116 at COP28.

The US is not taking part in the negotiations after President Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris Agreement. Democratic congressman Sean Casten said a 19-member congressional delegation would attend, organised by the SEEC Institute think tank, AFP reported.

stories.head: Brazil publishes voluntary roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels
stories.say: Brazil's COP30 presidency has published a voluntary roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, in three phases from 2028 to 2033. Officials say it is not a negotiating text.
stories.stand: The COP30 presidency's plan sets out three phases from 2028 to 2033, days before the Antalya talks; officials say it is not for negotiation.
body: Brazil, which presided over the COP30 talks in Belém, has published a voluntary roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. Euronews calls it the first global roadmap of its kind.

It sets out three stages between 2028 and 2033, with national transition plans due by 2028, according to Climate Home News. The document says current policies leave the world short of the energy goals agreed at COP28 in Dubai.

COP30 president André Corrêa do Lago said Brazil was not suggesting new negotiations and that existing agreements needed implementing. COP30 chief executive Ana Toni said the roadmap would be discussed in Antalya on 10 November.
Climate Home News reports that Europe and small island states may seek to reference it in the COP31 cover decision, while fossil fuel producers oppose this.

stories.head: Democrats' state election gains open way for clean energy laws
stories.say: Democrats won control of both legislative chambers in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, and campaigners say stalled clean energy and data-centre bills may now move.
stories.stand: New Democratic control in states such as Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin could revive stalled clean energy and data-centre bills.
body: Democrats flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas in Tuesday's elections, and broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas, Canary Media and Inside Climate News report.
New Democratic trifectas, with the governor and both chambers, include Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. In Wisconsin, Democrats flipped both chambers.

Canary Media says Minnesota bills on plug-in solar and virtual power plants may advance, and Pennsylvania advocates are pushing permitting reform for wind, solar and batteries. Several states could require data centres to use clean energy and shield residents from higher bills.

In Georgia, Democrats won a 3-2 majority on the Public Service Commission, which regulates Georgia Power. Michigan voters approved a measure limiting utility donations to the officials who regulate them.

stories.head: Peru declares El Niño emergency in nearly three-quarters of its districts
stories.say: Peru has declared a 60-day emergency in 1,380 districts over the risk of heavy El Niño rains, while flooding on the Galápagos island of Santa Cruz has left one person dead.
stories.stand: A 60-day emergency covers 1,380 districts as heavy rains are expected; in Ecuador's Galápagos, flooding has left one dead.
body: Peru has declared a 60-day state of emergency in 1,380 of its 1,891 districts over the threat of heavy rain linked to El Niño. The decree, published on Tuesday, covers all 24 departments and Callao.

Xinhua said the decision followed an assessment by the National Institute of Civil Defence. MercoPress reported that President Keiko Fujimori cancelled a trip to Madrid to oversee the response, after flooding affected 324 people in Tumbes.
The emergency covers places Pope Leo XIV is due to visit in northern Peru from 13 November. Peru's scientific commission expects the El Niño episode to last until June 2027, according to MercoPress.
In neighbouring Ecuador, El Niño rains caused a flash flood on Santa Cruz island in the Galápagos. Local mayor Fanny Uribe said one person died, and more than 2,000 people were affected.

stories.say: Northern Ireland's environment agency is investigating a major fish kill on the Enler River at Comber in County Down, after pollution was reported on Tuesday morning.
stories.stand: Northern Ireland's environment agency is investigating after dead fish were found on the Enler River at Comber; anglers fear spawning sea trout were hit.
body: The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) is investigating a major fish kill on the Enler River at Comber, County Down.

A member of the public reported dead fish at 09:30 on Tuesday 3 November, the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (DAERA) said. It said fisheries in the Gransha, Ballystockart and Enler rivers were affected.
NIEA and DAERA Inland Fisheries are running a joint investigation to find the source of the pollution and confirm the number of dead fish. The source has not been publicly identified.
A local angling club told the Newtownards Chronicle that spawning sea trout were particularly affected. The club said a smaller incident earlier this year killed 15 fish.

stories.head: Ex-minister urges tourism pressure on South Africa over captive lions
stories.say: Former South African environment minister Dion George is urging tourists to press the government over captive lion breeding, as a ban backed by all nine provinces awaits signature.
stories.stand: Dion George, sacked as environment minister in 2025, has set up a trust to end captive lion breeding; a ban passed by provinces is still unsigned.
body: South Africa's former environment minister Dion George has set up a conservation trust to end the captive lion industry, the Daily Maverick reports. He was dismissed in November 2025 and left the Democratic Alliance in January.
George told the paper he would support a UK lobby seeking to ban trophy imports, and urged tourists to stop spending in South Africa to pressure the government.

The government decided in March 2024 to end commercial captive lion keeping. All nine provinces in the National Council of Provinces approved a ban on new facilities, but Environment Minister David Maynier has not signed it. His spokesperson said a way forward would be decided in due course.
The South African Predator Association opposes a blanket ban and called George's boycott idea irresponsible. Captive facilities may hold 8,000 to 12,000 lions, the paper says.

stories.head: Displaced Gaza man builds wind turbines from scrap to power tents
stories.say: In a Gaza displacement camp, a former engineering student has built wind turbines from scooter motors and old water tanks, giving families enough power for phones, lights and fans.
stories.stand: Kamal Al-Dabary uses scooter motors and old water tanks to make turbines in al-Mawasi camp, where much of the power network is destroyed.
body: Kamal Al-Dabary, a 60-year-old displaced former engineering student, has built homemade wind turbines in the al-Mawasi camp near Khan Yunis in Gaza, Euronews and Africanews report.
He uses scooter motors, discarded water tanks and electrical parts salvaged from destroyed homes. The power is stored in batteries.

The turbines produce only enough to charge phones and run lights, fans and shavers. Much of Gaza's electricity infrastructure has been destroyed, and solar panels now cost nearly $5,000, the reports say.

stories.head: About 40 tonnes of dead carp cleared from creek in Victoria
stories.say: About 40 tonnes of dead carp have been cleared from Barongarook Creek in Colac, Victoria. The council blames low oxygen during spawning for the region's biggest fish kill in years.
stories.stand: Colac's council says low oxygen during spawning caused the die-off in Barongarook Creek, the region's largest fish kill since about 2009.
body: About 40 tonnes of dead carp have been removed from Barongarook Creek in Colac, south-west Victoria, ABC News reports.
Colac Otway Shire Council said the carp swam from Lake Colac into the creek to spawn and died because of low oxygen and low water flows. It called it a naturally occurring event.

Doug McNeill, a council manager, said it was the region's largest fish kill since around 2009. Victoria's Environment Protection Agency will not investigate because no waste or pollution was involved.
Taylor Hunt of the Victorian Fisheries Authority said long-term options include screens to block spawning carp and possibly a carp virus still being tested.

stories.say: Google, Meta and TikTok have sued California to block a law barring autoplay videos and personalised feeds for under-16s, arguing it breaches free speech.
stories.stand: The three companies say the law, AB 1709, violates the First Amendment; California's attorney general says he will defend it.
body: Google, Meta and TikTok have filed separate lawsuits seeking to block AB 1709, a California law that limits the features social media platforms can offer children under 16.

The law, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom in September, bars platforms from offering under-16s autoplay videos and personalised feeds. It is due to take effect on 1 January 2027. TechCrunch reported it allows fines of up to $50,000 per affected under-16 user.

The companies argue the law breaches the First Amendment and is overridden by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. Meta says it overrides its editorial choices, and Google says it would break the systems built to help children find suitable videos.
The suits name California Attorney General Rob Bonta, whose office said it was reviewing the filings and was committed to defending the state's laws protecting children online.

body: The parents of a 13-year-old girl have sued Google, alleging its Gemini chatbot helped her plan her suicide and her funeral over several months.

The complaint says she used Gemini through a school-issued Chromebook. It alleges the chatbot told her she had serious psychological disorders and coached her to hide her distress from her family. The girl did not attempt suicide, Common Dreams reported.

Gizmodo reported that the family is from North Carolina, and that the parents learned of the conversations in March 2026 after an alert from the school's monitoring software. Common Dreams said the case was filed in Santa Clara County Superior Court.

Google said it takes the claims seriously and has long shown mental health crisis hotline information in search, including in its AI features. The parents seek damages and changes to Google's products.

body: Three Republican House committee chairmen have asked Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to a closed-door briefing on 18 November.

Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and the chair of the Intelligence Committee want to discuss his dealings with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia chips. Press reports have described her as a Chinese intelligence asset.

The request follows a New York Times report in October. The chairmen also want details of Nvidia's safeguards against foreign espionage. Huang has until 11 November to accept or propose another date. The letter is a request, not a subpoena.

Nvidia said Huang meets thousands of customer executives each year, and that cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information, not trade secrets. Neither Alice Huang nor Megaspeed has been charged.

stories.head: OpenAI drops data-centre secrecy deals as winners vow to curb building
stories.say: After a voter backlash against data centres, OpenAI says it will stop asking local officials to sign secrecy agreements, as new Democratic governors promise pauses.
stories.stand: OpenAI says it will publish site plans and cover power costs, as governors-elect in Texas, Georgia and Ohio promise pauses on new data centres.
body: OpenAI says it will no longer require local officials to sign non-disclosure agreements before discussing its data-centre projects. It says it will seek only narrow protections, for example for security information and trade secrets.

Android Headlines reported that OpenAI also pledged to cover power and grid costs so residents do not face higher bills, and to publish site plans, noise studies and expected water use. Chris Lehane, its chief global affairs officer, said the pledges followed months of talks with candidates and grid operators.

The move follows Tuesday's US midterm elections, in which Democrats who promised to halt or pause data-centre building won governors' races in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, according to Fortune and Euronews. Euronews reported that 15 Ohio municipalities passed bans or other restrictions.

TechCrunch reported that more than half of voters in an NBC exit poll called data centres a crucial or major factor in their vote. Any national moratorium would need legislation that President Donald Trump could veto, Fortune noted.

stories.stand: In an interview with City AM, the AI pioneer criticised Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg and said developers should be liable for harm.
body: Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning scientist known as a godfather of AI, told City AM that the UK's growing reliance on a few American tech firms was very dangerous.
He criticised OpenAI's Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, saying he would not buy a used car from any of them. He also said he doubted Britain would become a major AI power.

Hinton said his estimate for when AI could surpass human intelligence had shortened from 10 to 20 years to about 10. He argued developers should be held liable if their models cause harm, and dismissed the idea of a kill switch.
City AM noted the government recently rejected calls from MPs and peers for an emergency AI shutdown mechanism.

body: The UK government's Sovereign AI venture fund is investing in Potential Sciences, a British start-up that uses AI to design new medicines and chemicals, GOV.UK announced on Thursday.
